title: Unicorn Fintech Founder Pravin Jadhav Says Top Bank Rejected His Home Loan, Called Him 'High Risk'
excerpt: The founder of $1.2 billion fintech firm Raise Financial Services shared the experience on social media, highlighting the irony of being denied credit by the very industry his company serves.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Pravin Jadhav's home loan was rejected by a bank, labeling him 'high risk' despite his fintech success.
  • The rejection highlights systemic issues in how banks assess creditworthiness for startup founders.
  • Jadhav previously built Paytm Money, India's largest investment platform, showcasing his industry credentials.
  • Many Indian startup founders face similar loan rejections due to traditional banking evaluation methods.
  • The incident sparks a broader conversation about the need for updated lending models in India's banking sector.
  • Pravin Jadhav, founder and CEO of $1.2 billion fintech firm Raise Financial Services, says a major Indian bank rejected his home loan application, classifying him as "high risk" because he is a startup founder.
  • Jadhav, who previously built Paytm Money into India's largest investment platform, shared the experience on X, sparking a broader conversation about how banks assess entrepreneurial borrowers.
  • Raise Financial operates Dhan, a fast-growing investment and trading platform backed by prominent investors including the founders of CRED, Flipkart and PhonePe.
  • The incident highlights a persistent gap between how traditional banks evaluate creditworthiness and the financial reality of India's startup founders.

The Irony of the Rejection

Pravin Jadhav runs a company that helps millions of Indians manage their money. But when he applied for a home loan from a top Indian bank, the institution turned him down — classifying the founder of a $1.2 billion fintech unicorn as a "high-risk" borrower.

Jadhav, founder and CEO of Raise Financial Services, which operates the popular investment platform Dhan, shared the experience on X, describing what he called the irony of a fintech founder being denied credit by the same banking system his company is working to modernize. The post resonated widely with India's startup community, where similar stories of loan rejections are common but rarely discussed publicly.

A Pattern Startup Founders Know Well

The problem is systemic rather than personal. Indian banks typically evaluate home loan applicants using standardized income verification models built around salaried employees. Startup founders, even those running billion-dollar companies, often draw modest salaries while holding significant equity stakes. Their income can be irregular, with compensation tied to company performance rather than fixed monthly pay.

"Startup founders, even those running billion-dollar companies, often draw modest salaries while holding significant equity stakes."

"Startup founders, even those running billion-dollar companies, often draw modest salaries while holding significant equity stakes."

For risk assessment algorithms designed around predictable paycheck cycles, this profile triggers red flags — regardless of the applicant's actual net worth or the strength of the business they've built. The result is that founders who create enormous economic value find themselves unable to pass the same credit checks that their own employees clear easily.

Jadhav's Track Record

Jadhav's credentials make the rejection particularly striking. Before founding Raise Financial Services, he built Paytm Money from the ground up as its founding Managing Director and CEO, turning it into India's largest investment platform. Prior to that, he founded Wishberg, an e-commerce venture that was acquired by Freecharge in 2014. He has two decades of experience across fintech, payments, e-commerce and mobile technology.

Raise Financial raised $22 million in its Series A round from BEENEXT and Mirae Asset Venture Investments. Its early backers read like a who's who of Indian tech: CRED founder Kunal Shah, Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy, PhonePe founders Sameer Nigam and Rahul Chari, Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham and several others.

"Building a billion-dollar company that serves millions of investors, and then being told you are too risky for a home loan — if that isn't irony, I don't know what is."

— Pravin Jadhav, on X, reacting to the home loan rejection

A Growing Conversation

Jadhav's public disclosure has reignited a familiar debate in India's startup ecosystem. While the country's banking sector has embraced digital payments and fintech partnerships, its lending models remain largely anchored in legacy risk-assessment frameworks that struggle to evaluate non-traditional income profiles.

For NRIs and members of the diaspora who have left corporate jobs to launch ventures, the issue is doubly relevant. Returning founders often face similar credit barriers, with banks unable or unwilling to evaluate entrepreneurial track records, overseas income histories or equity-based compensation.

The disconnect is notable at a time when India is positioning itself as a global startup hub. The country produced over 100 unicorns in the past five years, yet many of the founders behind those companies report difficulty accessing basic consumer financial products from the banks that profit from the broader tech boom.

Challenges for Startup Founders
›Traditional banks use salary-based models for loan assessments.
›Startup founders often have irregular income tied to company performance.
›Many founders report difficulties accessing basic financial products.
›Legacy risk-assessment frameworks fail to evaluate entrepreneurial income.

What Needs to Change

Industry observers say the fix requires banks to develop separate underwriting models for entrepreneurial borrowers — ones that consider equity holdings, company valuations, fundraising history and business cash flows alongside traditional salary metrics. Some new-age lenders have started offering founder-friendly products, but mainstream banks have been slow to adapt.

For now, Jadhav's experience serves as a pointed reminder: in India's booming startup economy, building a billion-dollar company is easier than getting a home loan to go with it.
